questions.sampleAnswer: Archaeological evidence at Pompeii and Herculaneum reveals much about food and dining. Common people would dine in taverns, selecting food from dolia set into benches, and Source A depicts a price list of food available for a food stall, including pork, bread, oil and cheese. This indicates that public dining using disposable income was available in Pompeii and Herculaneum. Frescoes and mosaics depict the types of food available to the local peoples. Carbonised seeds, bread and nuts from Herculaneum show us what people ate. Private houses contained triclinia, often highly decorated, showing that dinner parties were a common form of entertainment for wealthier people. Studies of bones have revealed that men in Herculaneum enjoyed a diet richer in seafood than women.

questions.sampleAnswer: Myths and legends were important for Egyptian religious beliefs in this period. The myth of Osiris focused on renewal and rebirth after death, providing a framework for religious beliefs that helped Egyptians to deal with difficult times and the catastrophe that could accompany the annual flood, which could bring both life and destruction. The myth was an explanation for the succession of kingship, as the living king, seen as the embodiment of Horus. Creation myths reinforced the religious notion of ma’at, that the gods had decreed good order and set things in their place. The most prominent myth involved Atum-Re creating Shu and Tefnut by himself, followed by a series of other sibling couples, representing various aspects of creation. Myths influenced Egyptian beliefs and practices regarding royal sibling marriages, possibly undertaken to mimic the relationships of the gods. These myths of renewal and rebirth also influenced festivals, such as the Opet festival, or the festival of Ptah, which celebrated his role in creation.

Art reveals information regarding trade and the impact of empire in this period. For example, the reliefs at Deir el-Bahri regarding the journey to Punt under Hatshepsut, show some of the materials accumulated from this trip, including incense trees. questions.sampleAnswer: Myths and legends relating to the Minoans tell us much about their society. The myth of the Minotaur tells of King Minos, a legendary ruler of Crete. He ruled over the Aegean people and established a thalassocracy. King Minos accepted tribute from his subjects, including Athens, and took young men and women every year to feed the Minotaur, a mythical half-man and half-bull monster which occupied the labyrinth under the palace at Knossos. This myth ties to the Minoan civilisation through the frequency of bull motifs, the use of Minos as a possible title for kings, the idea of the Minoan thalassocracy, and the maze of magazines under the Palace at Knossos which could be thought to represent a labyrinth. Some historians link the Minotaur with Baal-Moloch, a Canaanite god associated with child sacrifice. The myth of Daedalus and Icarus represents the importance of engineering and technology. Daedalus, whose name translates to ‘genius’, was credited with inventing carpentry as well as the saw, axe, plumbline, drill and glue. The Minoans were advanced in many forms of engineering, such as ashlar masonry, running water and toilets, roads and earthquake-proof housing.

questions.sampleAnswer: Myths and legends in Sparta were important as they created collective identity and justified the system of government. Lycurgus was a foundational myth, providing an origin story for the Great Rhetra which established social organisation and militaristic culture. Plutarch relates that Lycurgus brought the Spartan constitution as an oration from the Oracle at Delphi. He allegedly implemented new laws to focus Sparta’s efforts on militaristic control, communal living, and the production of strong warriors. His actions thus established the foundation of Sparta’s social, political and economic organisation. The Dioscuri were important for the existence of the dual monarchy, with symbols of the twins evident in archaeology. There are many references to the myth of the Trojan War at Sparta, such as the Menelaion, which reinforced societal expectations of militant men and beautiful women.

answersCouldInclude: Evidence reveals that Spartan society was highly stratified, despite calling its citizens homoioi.

Plutarch’s Life of Lycurgus reveals significant evidence about Spartan social structure during this period. This source provides the most detailed account of the organisation of Spartan society, with information on the structure of society and political organisation. Plutarch describes the ephorate, gerousia and ekklesia, as well as details on the dual kingship and the existence of an elite.

Evidence about women in Spartan society can be found in the sources of other Greek writers, such as Aristotle and Plutarch. These sources focus on how different Spartan women were to women in other Greek poleis. Plutarch also records the ‘Sayings of Spartan Women’, a text which reveals non-Spartan stereotypes about Spartan women linked to the militaristic nature of society.
There is limited evidence for the role of perioikoi in Spartan society, with few textual references.
Evidence from Xenophon demonstrates that perioikoi, helots and inferiors were unhappy with their position in the Spartan social system, revealed in the Kinadon conspiracy of 399 BC.
Archaeological evidence from Lakonia reveals the resources the perioikoi likely contributed to the economy, including marble, iron and murex.
